newsitem.title: DENMARK: Greenland's left-right home rule coalition splits.
newsitem.headline: Greenland's left-right home rule coalition splits.

text.p: Greenland's two-year-old left-right home rule coalition collapsed over a political row and talks on forming a new local government in the Arctic territory were due on Monday, Danish Radio news said on Sunday.

Following the last home rule elections in Greenland in March 1995, the centre-left Siumut party of local prime minister Lars Emil Johansen formed a coalition with the main right-wing Atassut grouping for a four-year term in office.
The two parties had a total of 22 seats in the 31-seat home rule assembly in Nuuk, the island capital.

The political crisis that brought the coalition down involved allegations by Siumut of incompetence on the part of the Knud Soerensen, an Atassut member and speaker of the local parliament, and demands for his resignation.

"We want to maintain our cooperation with Atassut but we demand that Knud Soerensen resign for his lack of competence in preparing the spring opening of parliament," Johansen told the Danish Ritzau news agency.

The start of the spring session of Greenland's parliament was suspended last Tuesday and postponed until May 2 and Siumut, the biggest party in the Nuuk assembly with 12 seats, threatened to annul the coalition if Atassut did not comply with its demands for Soerensen's resignation.

After a Saturday night deadline passed without Atassut dismissing Soerensen, Atassut said it would on Monday initiate negotiations on forming a new coalition with the far left Inuit Ataqatigiit (IA) grouping, which has six seats in the local legislature.
Icebound Greenland, the world's largest island, colonised by Denmark in 1721, has had home rule under the Danish crown since 1979.

IA advocates independence from Denmark, which has control of Greenland's foreign and defence policies and provides annual aid of three billion crowns ($460 million), 60 percent of the home rule government's revenue or 45 percent of gross domestic product.
Most of its 55,000 inhabitants are Inuit (eskimos).

Vulnerable fisheries account for 95 percent of Greenland's export income but the island is trying to diversify into tourism and has high hopes for exploitation of its underground zinc and gold resources and possibly rich offshore gas and oil deposits. ($ = 6.517 Danish Crowns)
